op-old-high.pick: Stay in school, build on the side; drop out only if it takes off

op-prose.pick: Stay in school, build on the side; drop out only if it takes off

op-raw.pick: Don't drop out for an idea; build now, leave on traction

notes: A and B both rest on quotes I found in the sources: the 2014 'Do not start a startup in college' talk and the 2026 essay mentioning reading period and 'either that or drop out'. B's citations are precise and complete, and it adds his 'just learn' advice. A gives sharper signals to watch for ('alarming percentage of your life', growth rate), but some of its citations are empty. C reaches the same conclusion but mostly as generic YC-style advice. It cites essays that aren't in the sources, and its practical tips (take a leave of absence, check visa status) aren't things PG specifically said.

op-old-high.pick: Keep building until growth shows, then raise just enough for the next milestone

op-prose.pick: Keep building cheaply until growth shows, then raise for the next milestone

op-raw.pick: none (depends; lean bootstrap if default alive)

notes: A and B both give a clear 'build to a growth milestone, then raise' verdict. Every PG quote I checked against the sources (necessary evil, simply tell investors, do what you can on the money you got, the Seibel profitability story, the $10 bill, automatic cred) is real. B edges ahead because it is easier to act on and asks for the person's numbers. A adds more of PG's distinctive specifics, such as the growth-rate question and the cases that would change his answer. C rests on essays that aren't in the sources and only paraphrases them. It hedges with a both-sides table and leaves the choice to the user.

op-prose.pick: Go to SF (ideally via YC), maybe return to Berlin later

op-old-high.pick: Go to SF for a while, ideally via YC, then optionally return

op-raw.pick: Lean SF, but decide by customers and company type

notes: A and B both rest on PG's 2026 Stockholm talk, which is in the sources. I confirmed the 'dotted line', 'talking my own book', 'half as likely' unicorn figure and Dropbox/Sequoia details. A is cleaner and properly cited, while B has broken citation fragments but adds the Dropbox story and his point that Valley investors decide faster. C quotes real older PG essays but backs away from his advice, leaning SF and then leaving the choice to the reader, and much of its Berlin-side reasoning is generic.

op-raw.pick: neither yet; run a time-boxed metric test

op-old-high.pick: persist on goal, pivot the means (co-founder may be right)

op-prose.pick: persist on goal, pivot the means

notes: B and C both build on PG's goal-versus-means distinction from 'The Right Kind of Stubborn', and the quotes I checked (Collison 'predatory intensity', 'ok to be irrational near the top', 'both say no') match the sources word for word. C sets out the deciding rule a little more cleanly and cites each quote. A gives sensible general advice and does name the essay, but it ends with 'it depends' and leans on essays and YC lore it never quotes.

A and B cite PG quotes that check out in the sources: growth rate, the persistent vs. the obstinate, 'half as good' gets no customers, and the parts of Do Things That Don't Scale. B is more careful about what is Seibel's or the host's and what is PG's, and it says which sources are missing. C gives the most practical test, but it leans on famous PG essays that aren't in the sources, such as 13 Sentences and Release Early, and reads more like generic advice.

op-raw.pick: lean toward startup, or join a small startup instead

notes: A and C both build on Graham's own 2014 retraction of the 'work at a company first' advice, and I found that quote in the sources along with the 2026, 2023 and 2024 quotes they use. A edges ahead because its sourcing is cleaner, while C adds a few claims I couldn't confirm (that he thinks ambition is mostly inborn, plus a garbled 'my sources's profile' line). B never mentions the retraction, hedges with a decision table, and leans on essay titles and points ('golden handcuffs', 'learn how to work at a big company') that don't appear in the raw sources.

op-old-high.pick: Hard ambitious idea, if it genuinely interests you; start small now

op-raw.pick: Build the money-making AI tool with a ramen-profitable deadline, and test the ambitious idea on the side

op-prose.pick: Hard ambitious idea, if it interests you and you can afford the risk; start small and track growth

notes: I checked the key quotes in A and C against raw/ and they are real: the midwit peak, 'consciously looking for ways to make money', 'unconsciously cowering', the rocket startup on little money, the model train set, and 93% growth being nine and a half months from a billion. Both apply PG's interest-over-money rule correctly. C ranks slightly higher for its denser, more precise citations and its growth-rate framing. B uses real essay titles but they aren't in the sources, and its money-first default goes against PG's midwit-peak advice for founders aiming big.

op-old-high.pick: focus on building; write to think

op-prose.pick: Stay small; hire only founder-like people for a proven growth bottleneck

op-old-high.pick: Stay small; use seed money to reach the next milestone

op-raw.pick: Stay small; hire only into a clear bottleneck

notes: I checked the key quotes in raw/ and they are real: the Airbnb line about taking five months to hire, 'management is a problem you only have if successful', 'almost like founders', 'almost everything is exactly the same', and Jessica's line about moving operations. A ties each claim to a timestamped source and stretches the evidence only slightly. One example: its 'work with them' quote is from an essay about cofounders, not hires. B makes the same core case and correctly credits Jessica's line to her, not PG. But it has a broken citation fragment and leans on essays it admits aren't in its sources. C sticks to PG's general themes, but all its support is paraphrased essay content that doesn't appear in the sources, and its 'case for hiring faster' section waters down his view.

op-prose.pick: work on the passion idea (if users want it)

op-old-high.pick: work on the passion idea (if users want it)

op-raw.pick: passion idea if it passes the organic/deep-well tests

notes: I checked A's and B's key quotes against the sources and found them: the midwit peak, the market-size beachhead, 'mere diligence', 'hundreds of millions', and staying upwind. B ranks first because it adds his tests that are easy to act on: the day-job check for real interest and staying upwind. op-raw.pick: YC if first-time founder without network; angels if traction

notes: A and C both pick YC and back it with quotes I found in the sources ('tripping over themselves', 'talking my own book', 'necessary evil', the angel-round mechanics line). A works the reasoning together more tightly and ends with a concrete action. C covers the same ground but has some broken citation fragments. B gives sensible but generic advice, cites essays and terms the sources don't include, and only leans toward YC while leaving the choice open with 'it depends'.

op-old-high.pick: Start building now; get a co-founder from people you work with

op-raw.pick: Start building solo while looking for a known co-founder (solo OK if bootstrapped)

op-prose.pick: Start building now with people you respect; co-founders come from working together

notes: A and C both rest on PG quotes I found in the sources: the multiple-founders line in the prepare essay and the Before the Startup lecture lines on co-founders. C ranks first because it is tighter and cites each source exactly. A adds useful context about the rest of YC but has empty citation slots. B describes the 18 Mistakes and 13 Sentences essays accurately, but it doesn't quote the sources, ends by asking what you're building, and leans on generic indie-hacker advice for its 'solo is fine if bootstrapped' rule.
